After the leaves have fallen, we return To a plain sense of things. It is as if We had come to an end of the imagination, Inanimate in an inert savoir. The greenhouse never so badly needed paint. The chimney is fifty years old and slants to one side. A fantastic effort has failed, a repetition In a repetitiousness of men and flies. Yet the absence of the imagination had Itself to be imagined. outputs.L1:
After the leaves have fallen, we return  
to a plain sense of things. It is as if  
we had come to the end of imagination,  
inanimate in an inert savoir.

It is difficult even to choose the adjective  
for this blank cold, this sadness without cause.  
The great structure has become a minor house.  
No turban walks across the diminished floors.  
The greenhouse has never so badly needed paint.  
The chimney is fifty years old and leans to one side.

A fantastic effort has failed—a repetition  
within the repetitiousness of men and flies.  
Yet the absence of imagination  
had itself to be imagined.

The great pond—the plain sense of it,  
without reflections or leaves; mud;  
water like dirty glass, expressing a kind of silence,  
the silence of a rat emerging to look;  
the great pond and its waste of lilies—all this  
had to be imagined as inevitable knowledge,  
required as necessity itself requires.
outputs.L2:
Once the trees are bare, we confront the world in its simplest form, as though imagination has exhausted itself and left us lifeless within a stagnant kind of knowledge. Even finding a word for this empty chill—this unprovoked sorrow—is hard. What was once a grand building now seems like a modest dwelling. No turbaned figure crosses its diminished rooms. The greenhouse is in desperate need of fresh paint, and the fifty-year-old chimney tilts sideways. Some magnificent undertaking has collapsed, becoming merely another cycle in the monotonous repetitions of people and flies.

Still, even this lack of imagination could only be understood by imagining it. The large pond had to be conceived in its bare reality: stripped of reflections and leaves, filled with mud, its water resembling grimy glass, conveying a peculiar hush—the quiet of a rat emerging to look around. The pond, together with its ruined lilies, had to be envisioned as unavoidable knowledge, something demanded with the force of necessity itself.
outputs.L3:
After the leaves have fallen, the world seems stripped of color, ornament, and imaginative vitality, returning to a stark and unembellished reality. The speaker struggles to put this condition into words: what remains is a blank coldness and a sadness without any obvious cause, as though the imagination itself has been exhausted. The surrounding landscape reflects this decline. What may once have seemed grand or full of promise has deteriorated into a diminished house, a neglected greenhouse, and a chimney leaning precariously in the distance.

Yet this failure of imaginative energy is not presented as a unique or final catastrophe. Instead, it belongs to the repetitive cycles of both human experience and the natural world. Just as leaves grow and fall, the imagination flourishes, weakens, and may eventually renew itself. Paradoxically, even the plain, silent, and desolate reality that remains cannot be encountered without imagination. The mind must conceive this emptiness and accept it as a necessary form of knowledge—a difficult recognition of the world as it appears when comforting illusions and embellishments have fallen away.
outputs.L4:
Wallace Stevens’s “The Plain Sense of Things” confronts the possibility of a world from which imagination seems to have disappeared. The poem presents a late-autumn landscape marked by exhaustion and decline: leaves have fallen, the house appears neglected, the greenhouse is in ruins, and the pond lies barren beneath an empty sky. Its language is restrained and deliberately unadorned, as if the speaker were trying to perceive reality without metaphor, embellishment, or emotional consolation. In this setting, both the natural world and the human structures within it seem stripped of vitality and meaning.

Yet the poem gradually complicates the idea that reality can ever be apprehended in a purely “plain” way. The decaying house and vacant pond are not simply neutral objects; they become signs of absence, desolation, and imaginative failure. To describe the world as empty already requires the mind to shape what it sees into a meaningful pattern. The poem’s bleakness is therefore itself an imaginative achievement. Even when imagination appears exhausted, it continues to organize experience and give form to loss.

The poem ultimately reveals a paradox: the “plain sense” of things cannot exist independently of the imagination that perceives it. Emptiness must be conceived, barrenness must be represented, and the absence of meaning must itself be made meaningful. Stevens thus suggests that imagination is not merely a decorative escape from reality. It is an inescapable means of understanding reality, present even in our starkest and most disillusioned perceptions of the world.
outputs.L5:
**After**

After the last train vanished beyond the hill, the station became strangely still. An inanimate clock watched over the empty platform, its hands frozen at midnight. For years, no one came to repair it.

Then, one winter evening, a traveler arrived and sat beneath the silent clock. He was not waiting for a train. He had come for the memories—of departures, reunions, and promises once made there.

For the first time in decades, the clock began to tick.
